title: Dig under the wall
hookLine: the principle of saving life shapes modern debates; answers differ by community
carry: live by them, not die by them
last: REASON FROM THE NEAREST OLD CASE.

cards: Shabbat afternoon. A wall comes down, and stones cover a corner of the courtyard. Is someone under there?
Nobody's sure. If someone is, are they alive? Nobody knows.
On a day when work stops, when even moving stones is restricted, what happens next? The Mishnah does not hesitate. Clear the stones.
Even if it's doubtful anyone is there. Even if it's doubtful they're alive. Even if nobody knows whether the person under them is Jewish or not.

teach.b: Saving life first. In Hebrew, pikuach nefesh. You met it in year two; today, how far it reaches.
First, doubt is enough. The Mishnah in tractate Yoma says that wherever there is a doubt of danger to life, it sets Shabbat aside. You don't need certainty before you act.
Second, the source. The Talmud asks where this comes from, and offers several answers.
One it lands on is a verse in Leviticus about God's laws: "which if a man do, he shall live by them." Live by them, the Talmud says, and not die by them. The commandments are meant for living.
Third, the limits. Saving life sets aside almost everything, but not quite everything.
The Talmud names a few things a person may not do even to save their own life, among them taking another person's life. One life is not bought with another. Fourth, today.
This principle sits in the middle of hard modern questions. When must a sick person eat on Yom Kippur? The Mishnah already says a sick person is fed when experts say so.
How hard should doctors push at the end of a life?

teach.h: LIVE BY THEM, NOT DIE BY THEM.
teach.b: Here, honestly, answers differ, between communities and within them. What they share is the starting point: life comes first, and the arguments are about what that requires. A rule built for living.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat and the fasts set them aside when a life may be in danger, calling for help, driving to a hospital or eating on Yom Kippur when doctors say so. Families facing medical decisions often consult a rabbi alongside their doctors.

o: the rule that saving a life sets aside nearly every law
a prayer said for someone who is very sick
a rule that only doctors may work on the Sabbath

games.q: saving life first — tap the pairs.
p: is enough to set Shabbat aside

s: on Shabbat, you wait until nightfall to dig someone out
the Mishnah says clear the stones at once, even if it's doubtful anyone is there.
the Mishnah says to dig even when nobody knows if the person is Jewish
it lists that doubt too, and the answer is still: dig.
saving a life permits absolutely anything
the Talmud names limits, among them taking another person's life.

games.q: it's Shabbat. a wall has collapsed in the courtyard, and someone may be under the stones. nobody knows if anyone's there, or if they're alive. what do you do?
o: wait until Shabbat ends, then dig.
dig only if you're sure someone's alive.
games.why: the Mishnah says clear the stones, even in doubt. wherever there's a doubt of danger to life, it sets Shabbat aside.

practice: Bring to mind one person who might sit beside you if you were ever very sick, and see their face.
Ask yourself, quietly and without hurry, what you'd want them to know about treatment, comfort, and who should decide if you can't; you don't need answers now.
If any of this weighs on you, or you're in danger yourself, you don't have to hold it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency help.
